blocks.text: To this belong these words of Columella, book 9, chapter 11: He covers himself, as if admiring himself, with the jewelled feathers of his tail, and when he does this, he is said to "wheel." And those of Pliny, book 10, chapter 20: When praised he spreads out his jewelled colours, especially facing the sun, because thus they shine more brilliantly. And a little later: And he gathers into a heap all the eyes of his feathers, which he delights to have looked at. But it is above all the Greeks who take pleasure in this theme, and spread the sails of their eloquence as widely [II, 841] as the peacock spreads his feathers. Among them Moschus, being older, is also simpler, and has only this, Idyll. 2:
Ὄρνις ἀγαλλόμενος πτερύγων πολυανθέϊ χροιῇ, [Ornis agallomenos pterygōn polyantheï chroiē,]

A bird exulting in the flowery colour of its feathers. But Dio says far more in the Olympic oration, where he describes the peacock ἐπαφόμενον, καὶ ἐπιδεικνύοντα τὸ κάλλος τῶν πτερῶν, ὅταν ἁβρύνεται πρὸς τὴν θήλειαν, ἀνακλάσας τὴν οὐρὰν, καὶ περιστήσας αὐτῷ πανταχόθεν, ὥσπερ εὐειδὲς θέατρον, ἤ τινι γραφῇ μιμηθέντα οὐρανὸν ποικίλον ἄστροις· [epaphomenon, kai epideiknyonta to kallos tōn pterōn, hotan habrynetai pros tēn thēleian, anaklasas tēn ouran, kai peristēsas autō pantachothen, hōsper eueides theatron, ē tini graphē mimēthenta ouranon poikilon astrois] exalting himself and showing off the beauty of his feathers, when he plays the lover to the female, bending back his tail and setting it round himself on every side, like a handsome theatre, or like a painting imitating the heaven studded with stars. [col. 241] And below: Ἐν μέσῳ δὲ μάλα ἥσυχον καὶ ἀτρεμοῦντα παρέχει ἑαυτὸν θεάσασθαι, ὥσπερ ἐν πομπῇ περιστρεφόμενον· [En mesō de mala hēsychon kai atremounta parechei heauton theasasthai, hōsper en pompē peristrephomenon] In the middle he offers himself to be viewed quite still and motionless, as if carried round in a procession. In the first passage of Dio, for ἀνακλάσας τὴν οὐρὰν [anaklasas tēn ouran], the most noble Monsieur de Grentemesnil advises reading ἀνακλίσας [anaklisas] opening, or spreading out; which pleases me very much. Aelian, History of Animals, book 5, chapter 21: Ὁ ταὼς οἶδεν ὀρνίθων ὡραιότατος ὢν, καὶ ἔνθα οἱ τὸ κάλλος κάθηται, καὶ τοῦτο οἶδε, καὶ ἐπ' αὐτῷ κομᾷ, καὶ σοβαρός ἐστι, καὶ θαῤῥεῖ τοῖς πτεροῖς, ἅπερ οὖν αὐτῷ καὶ κόσμον παρατίθησι, καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξωθεν φόβον ἀποστέλλει. [Ho taōs oiden ornithōn hōraiotatos ōn, kai entha hoi to kallos kathētai, kai touto oide, kai ep' autō koma, kai sobaros esti, kai tharrei tois pterois, haper oun autō kai kosmon paratithēsi, kai pros tous exōthen phobon apostellei.] The peacock knows that he is the most beautiful of all birds, and he knows very well where his beauty lies, and prides himself on it, and is haughty, and trusts in his plumage, which both gives him adornment and strikes others with a kind of fear. And below: Ὅπως ἔχει τῆς εἰς τὴν ἐπίδειξιν ἀφθονίας παρίστησιν. ἐᾷ γὰρ ἐμπλησθῆναι τῆς θέας τὸν παρεστῶτα, καὶ ἑαυτὸν περιάγει, δεικνὺς φιλοπόνως τὸ τῆς πτερώσεως πολύμορφον. [Hopōs echei tēs eis tēn epideixin aphthonias paristēsin. ea gar emplēsthēnai tēs theas ton parestōta, kai heauton periagei, deiknys philoponōs to tēs pterōseōs polymorphon.] He shows how great a desire he has to display himself. For he lets the spectator take his fill of the sight of him, and turns himself in every direction, showing with great zeal the variety of his feathers. Especially in flowery, springtime meadows, as Lucian observes in On the Hall: Οὗτος, ἐκπετάσας τὰ πτερὰ, καὶ ἀναδείξας τῷ ἡλίῳ, καὶ τὴν οὐρὰν ἐπάρας, καὶ πάντοθεν αὐτῷ περιστήσας, ἐπιδείκνυται τὰ ἄνθη τὰ αὐτοῦ, καὶ τὸ ἔαρ τῶν πτερῶν, ὥσπερ αὐτὸν προκαλοῦντος τοῦ λειμῶνος ἐς τὴν ἅμιλλαν. [Houtos, ekpetasas ta ptera, kai anadeixas tō hēliō, kai tēn ouran eparas, kai pantothen autō peristēsas, epideiknytai ta anthē ta autou, kai to ear tōn pterōn, hōsper auton prokalountos tou leimōnos es tēn hamillan.] He, with his feathers spread out and shown to the sun, and his tail raised and expanded all around, displays his own flowers too, and the springtime of his feathers, as if he were challenged to this contest by the meadow. Thus in the first book of Achilles Tatius there is described in a garden ὁ ταὼς τοῖς ἄνθεσιν περισύρων τὸ πτερὸν [ho taōs tois anthesin perisyrōn to pteron], the peacock spreading his feathers around the flowers. But by this same art he also attracts the females. In the same place, a little below: Ὅταν ἐπαγαγέσθαι θέλῃ τὴν ἐρωμένην, τότε οὕτως καλλωπίζεται· [Hotan epagagesthai thelē tēn erōmenēn, tote houtōs kallōpizetai] When he wishes to attract the female he loves, then he adorns himself in this way. And of the peahen next to him: Ταύτῃ νῦν οὗτος τὸ κάλλος ἐπιδείκνυται, λειμῶνα πτερῶν· [Tautē nyn houtos to kallos epideiknytai, leimōna pterōn] To her he now displays his beauty, namely the [II, 842] meadow of his feathers. Hence Nazianzen, Oration 34: Ταῖς θηλείαις, ὥς φασι, καλλωπίζεται, τὸν αὐχένα διάρας, καὶ τὸ πτερὸν κυκλοτέρως, περιστήσας τὸ χρυσαυγὲς, καὶ κατάστερον, θεατρίζει τὸ κάλλος τοῖς ἐράσταις μετὰ σοβαροῦ τοῦ βαδίσματος. [Tais thēleiais, hōs phasi, kallōpizetai, ton auchena diaras, kai to pteron kykloterōs, peristēsas to chrysauges, kai katasteron, theatrizei to kallos tois erastais meta sobarou tou badismatos.] He shows himself off, as they say, to his females; and, with neck raised and his feathers, which reflect the gleam of gold and stars, arranged in a circle, he sets forth his beauty for his lovers to view, as in a theatre, with a kind of proud gait. In the same way Eustathius in the Hexaëmeron: Τῶν πτερῶν ἐπιδείξας τὸ θέατρον ἐπάγεται πρὸς συνουσίαν τὴν θήλειαν, ὥσπερ λειμῶνα τὸν καλλωπισμὸν τοῦτον ἐπιδεικνὺς αὐτῇ. [Tōn pterōn epideixas to theatron epagetai pros synousian tēn thēleian, hōsper leimōna ton kallōpismon touton epideiknys autē.] Displaying the theatre of his feathers he entices the female to mating, exhibiting this adornment to her like a meadow. For more on the same theme see the Iambics of Philes on the peacock, which begin thus:
Πτεροῖς ὁ ταὼς γαυριῶν πολυχρόοις, [Pterois ho taōs gauriōn polychroois,]
